content.title: About
content.content: Corn syrup is a thick, sweet syrup made from corn starch through hydrolysis. It is widely used in the food industry as a sweetener, stabilizer, and texture enhancer in baked goods, candies, and beverages.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Corn syrup is often classified as high‑fructose corn syrup (HFCS) when it contains more than 55 % fructose.
It is cheaper than sugar thanks to the abundant production of corn in the United States and other countries.
The syrup can be light (low glucose) or dark (with added caramel for color and flavor).
Its mass adoption in soft drinks during the 1970s contributed to the rise of sugar consumption in the US.
Corn syrup is a common ingredient in barbecue sauces, ketchup, and marinades.

items.title: Quick source of energy
items.content: Contains simple sugars that are rapidly absorbed, helping to quickly replenish glycogen stores.

items.title: Improves baked goods texture
items.content: Retains moisture in breads and cakes, keeping them softer and fresher longer.

items.title: Stabilizer in confections
items.content: Prevents sugar crystallization in ice cream and frozen desserts.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Excessive intake can contribute to weight gain, tooth decay, and metabolic disturbances.

items.title: Fructose load
items.content: Large amounts of fructose may raise blood triglycerides and stress the liver.

items.title: Corn allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience allergic reactions to corn‑derived products.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Add corn syrup to doughs, sauces, marinades, drinks, ice cream, and confectionery. It works well as a liquid sweetener in recipes that require moisture and softness.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a tightly sealed container in a cool, dry place away from direct light. Properly stored, it lasts 12–24 months. Discard if the syrup changes odor, color, or taste.

content.title: About
content.content: Ice cream cone (NFS) is a classic dessert consisting of sweet creamy ice cream placed inside a crunchy waffle cone. The cone provides a pleasant textural contrast, and the ice cream can be any flavor: vanilla, chocolate, strawberry, etc.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first waffle cone was invented in 1904 in the United States.
The term “NFS” (Not For Sale) is often used in culinary contests to denote experimental flavors.
Waffle cones are made from batter baked in a special mold, giving them a light, crisp texture.
Ice cream cones are frequently served with sprinkles, sauces, or fruit for extra flavor.
In some countries the cone is considered a separate product, not just packaging.

items.title: Source of calcium
items.content: The dairy base of ice cream provides calcium essential for bone health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Dairy products are rich in vitamins B2 and B12, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Quick energy
items.content: Sugar and fat in ice cream supply rapid energy, useful on hot days.

items.title: Mood boost
items.content: Consuming sweet treats can improve mood by triggering serotonin release.

items.title: Fruit additions
items.content: If the ice cream contains fruit pieces, it adds a modest amount of vitamin C.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Large amounts of sugar can contribute to weight gain and increase diabetes risk.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: People with lactose intolerance may experience discomfort after eating dairy ice cream.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Allergy to casein or whey requires avoiding traditional ice cream.

items.title: Trans fats in cones
items.content: Some commercial cones may contain partially hydrogenated oils.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy the ice cream cone immediately after serving while the cone stays crunchy. Add sprinkles, chocolate sauce, nuts, or fresh berries to taste.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store ice cream in a freezer at –18 °C or lower. Keep waffle cones in a dry, airtight container to prevent them from becoming soggy.

content.title: About
content.content: Luncheon meat (also known as canned meat) is a ready‑to‑eat meat product made from beef, pork or a mixture of both, seasoned with salt, spices and stabilizers. It is packed in a sealed can and can be stored at room temperature for extended periods.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first canned meat recipes appeared in the United States in the early 20th century.
The term “luncheon meat” originated because the product was often served during lunch breaks.
Canned meat is popular for camping, military rations and emergency supplies.
Nitrites are commonly added to give the characteristic pink colour and to extend shelf life.
In different countries the product is known by various names: “spam”, “canned meat”, “meat loaf”.

items.title: Protein source
items.content: Luncheon meat provides about 12–15 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Iron from the meat helps form hemoglobin and prevents anemia.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The product supplies thiamine, riboflavin and niacin, which are essential for metabolism.

items.title: Energy dense
items.content: Its high fat and protein content offers a quick source of energy.

items.title: Long shelf life
items.content: Sealed cans allow storage without refrigeration for several years.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Large amounts of salt can raise blood pressure; people with hypertension should limit intake.

items.title: Nitrites and preservatives
items.content: Some additives may cause allergic reactions or increase the risk of carcinogen formation with long‑term use.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: High levels of saturated fat may contribute to cardiovascular disease.

items.title: Meat allergy
items.content: A minority of individuals may be allergic to beef or pork.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The meat can be eaten straight from the can, sliced for sandwiches, added to salads, soups or stir‑fries. It is often warmed in a pan or microwave before serving.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep unopened cans in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, store the remaining meat in a sealed container in the refrigerator and consume within 5 days.

pasta-with-tomato-based-sauce-seafood-an.title: Pasta with tomato-based sauce, seafood, and added vegetables

content.title: About
content.content: A home recipe for pasta tossed in a tomato‑based sauce, assorted seafood (shrimp, mussels, calamari) and added vegetables (bell pepper, zucchini, spinach). The pasta is cooked al dente, while the sauce is slightly spicy, enriched with garlic and basil.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Tomato sauces in Italian cuisine are traditionally made from ripe tomatoes, olive oil, and fresh herbs.
Seafood is a rich source of omega‑3 fatty acids that support heart health.
The pasta‑seafood combination is popular along the Mediterranean coast, especially in coastal Italy.
Adding vegetables boosts fiber content and makes the dish more filling without extra calories.
Homemade sauce retains more vitamins than store‑bought versions.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Seafood and pasta together provide a complete amino‑acid profile that supports tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Cardiovascular support
items.content: Omega‑3 from fish and antioxidants from tomatoes help lower LDL cholesterol.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: Tomatoes supply vitamin C and lycopene, vegetables add vitamin A and folate, seafood contributes zinc and iodine.

items.title: Fiber
items.content: Vegetables and whole‑grain pasta aid digestion and promote satiety.

items.title: Low glycemic impact
items.content: Using durum‑wheat pasta results in a slower rise in blood sugar.

items.title: Seafood allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience severe allergic reactions to shrimp, mussels, or calamari.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: If the sauce is made with canned tomato puree or broth, salt levels can be high.

items.title: Foodborne illness
items.content: Seafood must be cooked thoroughly to avoid bacterial contamination.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: Traditional pasta contains gluten; gluten‑free alternatives are needed for celiac disease.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the pasta hot, topped with the tomato‑seafood‑vegetable sauce. Sprinkle with grated Parmesan, fresh basil, or a drizzle of olive oil. The dish pairs well with a light white wine.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for 2‑3 days. When reheating, add a splash of water or broth to keep the sauce from drying out. Only the sauce (without pasta) is suitable for freezing.

content.title: About
content.content: Potato patty is a ready‑to‑cook product made from grated potatoes, often combined with onion, spices and breadcrumbs. It is convenient for quick frying or baking and can be served as a side dish or a main course.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Potato patties originated in the United States in the early 20th century as a way to use surplus potatoes.
Variants may contain cheese, carrots, or herbs, allowing a wide range of flavors.
They are commonly sold frozen, which preserves taste and nutritional quality.
In Russia they are popular as pre‑made “potato pancakes” available in most supermarkets.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Potatoes are rich in starch, providing sustained energy and a feeling of fullness.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Potato patty contains vitamin B6 and folate, important for metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Potassium
items.content: Potassium helps regulate fluid balance and supports heart function.

items.title: Low fat when prepared healthily
items.content: If baked or steamed without excessive oil, the patty remains a low‑fat option.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion and helps maintain stable blood sugar levels.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Ready‑made patties often contain added salt; people with hypertension should watch portion size.

items.title: Fat when fried
items.content: Frying in a lot of oil significantly increases calorie count.

items.title: Allergens in additives
items.content: Some versions include dairy, gluten or eggs, which must be considered for food allergies.

items.title: Temperature control
items.content: Insufficiently heated patties may retain bacteria, especially if raw ingredients are present.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Patty can be pan‑fried, baked in the oven, or steamed. Serve with sauce, sour cream, a vegetable salad, or use as a filling for sandwiches.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep frozen patties in a freezer at –18 °C. After thawing, use within 1–2 days and store in the refrigerator at 0–4 °C.

content.title: About
content.content: Tartar sauce is a cold condiment made from mayonnaise mixed with finely chopped cornichons, capers, onion, herbs, and sometimes mustard. It has a creamy texture and a mildly tangy, savory flavor that pairs well with fish, seafood, and fried meats.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The name “tartar” comes from the French word for the sauce, but it has no relation to steak tartare.
Traditional recipes include cornichons (small pickled gherkins) and capers, which give the sauce its characteristic bite.
In the United States the sauce is commonly served with fish and chips, while in Europe it often accompanies seafood and steak dishes.
Many variations exist, such as yogurt‑based lighter versions, garlic‑infused, or herb‑rich twists.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Capers and cornichons provide vitamin B6 and niacin, which support metabolic processes.

items.title: Source of healthy fats
items.content: The mayonnaise base, usually made with vegetable oil, supplies monounsaturated fats.

items.title: Contains probiotics
items.content: When fermented ingredients like pickled onions are used, the sauce can contribute beneficial gut bacteria.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: Because it is mayonnaise‑based, tartar sauce is calorie‑dense and can contribute to weight gain if eaten in excess.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Traditional mayonnaise contains eggs, making the sauce unsuitable for people with egg allergies.

items.title: Sodium level
items.content: Capers and cornichons add a notable amount of salt, which may be a concern for those with hypertension.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve tartar sauce chilled as a dip for fried fish, seafood, chicken nuggets, or vegetable sticks. It also works well as a spread on sandwiches and as a dressing for salads.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the sauce in an airtight container in the refrigerator and consume within 5–7 days. Discard if you notice off‑smell, discoloration, or mold.
